pathophysiology.summary: Pneumonia is the leading infectious cause of death in Indian children under 5. Bacteria (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae; Staphylococcus aureus after measles or with boils) and viruses infect the alveoli, causing exudate that stiffens the lungs and impairs gas exchange. The child breathes faster and, as compliance falls, the lower chest wall is drawn in on inspiration. India's IMNCI approach classifies illness at the bedside without X-ray: general danger signs (convulsions, unable to drink, lethargy, vomiting everything) mean severe pneumonia needing referral and injectable antibiotics; fast breathing (50/min or more at 2–11 months; 40/min or more at 12–59 months) and/or lower chest indrawing without danger signs means pneumonia treatable at home with oral amoxicillin for 5 days when oxygen saturation is above 92% and the child can feed. Hypoxaemia below 90–92% needs oxygen. Children with severe acute malnutrition are treated as severe pneumonia even without chest indrawing.
keyMechanisms: Alveolar infection and exudate reduce lung compliance.
Reduced compliance causes fast breathing and lower chest indrawing.
Ventilation–perfusion mismatch causes hypoxaemia.
Staphylococcal infection causes pneumatocoeles, empyema and pneumothorax.

pathophysiology.summary: Measles is a highly contagious paramyxovirus infection spread through respiratory droplets and air; one case can infect up to 18 others, and patients are infectious from 4 days before to 4 days after the rash. India is pursuing measles–rubella elimination, but outbreaks still occur where immunisation coverage is low. After 7–14 days' incubation, a prodrome of fever, cough, coryza and conjunctivitis with Koplik spots is followed 3–5 days later by a maculopapular rash spreading from face to trunk and limbs. The virus causes immune suppression ('immune amnesia') and depletes vitamin A, which explains the complications that cause most deaths: pneumonia (including staphylococcal), croup, diarrhoea and dehydration, otitis media, corneal ulceration and blindness, malnutrition and encephalitis. Malnourished, vitamin A–deficient and HIV-infected children and pregnant women are at highest risk. There is no specific antiviral; two age-based doses of vitamin A on consecutive days reduce complications, and complications are treated as they arise. Two doses of measles-containing vaccine prevent disease.
keyMechanisms: Respiratory infection spreads to lymphoid tissue and epithelium, producing rash and enanthem.
Measles causes immune suppression, predisposing to secondary bacterial infection.
Vitamin A depletion causes eye damage and increases mortality.
Central nervous system involvement causes encephalitis and, years later, subacute sclerosing panencephalitis.

pathophysiology.summary: Diphtheria is caused by toxin-producing Corynebacterium diphtheriae spread by respiratory droplets and contact. Outbreaks continue in India among under-immunised children and adolescents. Bacteria multiply on the tonsils, pharynx, larynx or nose and form a grey-white adherent pseudomembrane that bleeds if dislodged; local oedema and nodes cause a 'bull neck' and can obstruct the airway. Absorbed exotoxin blocks protein synthesis in heart and nerve cells, causing myocarditis with conduction block and heart failure about 2–7 weeks after onset, and neuropathy (palatal, ocular, respiratory and limb weakness) 1–3 months after onset. Diagnosis is clinical, so treatment must not wait for culture. Diphtheria antitoxin neutralises only unbound toxin and must be given early as a single dose after hypersensitivity testing; antibiotics (penicillin or a macrolide) for 14 days eradicate the organism and stop transmission. Patients are isolated, close contacts receive prophylaxis, and everyone's immunisation is completed.

Exotoxin inhibits protein synthesis in myocardium and nerves.
Myocarditis appears 2–7 weeks and neuropathy 1–3 months after onset.
Antitoxin neutralises only circulating, unbound toxin, so timing matters.

pathophysiology.summary: Tetanus results from contamination of a wound, the umbilical stump or an unsterile procedure with spores of Clostridium tetani, which germinate in low-oxygen tissue and release tetanospasmin. The toxin travels to the spinal cord and brainstem and blocks inhibitory (GABA and glycine) neurotransmission, so motor neurones fire unopposed. This produces trismus, rigidity of the face, neck, trunk and limbs, and painful generalised spasms triggered by stimuli, with consciousness preserved. Autonomic instability usually appears in the second week. Neonatal tetanus follows unclean delivery or cord care: a baby who sucked normally becomes irritable and unable to suck, then rigid with spasms between days 3 and 28. India was certified as having eliminated maternal and neonatal tetanus in 2015, but cases still occur in unimmunised people. Short incubation and a short interval to first spasm predict death. Treatment combines immunoglobulin to neutralise unbound toxin, metronidazole to eradicate the organism, wound care, benzodiazepines to control spasms, quiet nursing with nasogastric feeding, and airway support. Tetanus does not confer immunity, so survivors are vaccinated.
keyMechanisms: Spores germinate in devitalised tissue and release tetanospasmin.
Toxin blocks inhibitory neurotransmission, causing rigidity and spasms.
Autonomic involvement causes labile blood pressure and arrhythmia in the second week.
Spasms of larynx and respiratory muscles cause asphyxia and aspiration.

clinicalManagement.title: Nurse and protect the airway
actions: Dark, quiet room; minimal handling; reposition every 3–4 hours; blindfold neonates.
Nasogastric tube for feeds, fluids and drugs; expressed breast milk every 3 hours for neonates.
Keep suction, bag-mask and intubation equipment ready.

clinicalManagement.title: Neutralise toxin and eradicate infection
actions: Human tetanus immunoglobulin intramuscularly as a single dose.
Metronidazole intravenously; clean and debride the wound (do not excise the umbilical stump).

clinicalManagement.title: Control spasms
actions: Diazepam intravenously, titrated to spasms while respiratory rate stays above the age minimum; continuous infusion if spasms persist; magnesium sulfate as an adjunct reduces benzodiazepine and ventilation needs.
Wean diazepam gradually through the nasogastric tube; never stop abruptly.

clinicalManagement.title: Vaccinate
actions: Start tetanus vaccination after recovery; for neonatal tetanus vaccinate the mother.

adjustments: Paediatric: Same dose for neonates and children (MSF).
Penicillin allergy: Not a beta-lactam; penicillin allergy does not change this medicine.
CKD: No change.
CLD: No change.

pathophysiology.summary: Birth asphyxia — failure to establish breathing at birth — is a major cause of newborn death and brain injury in India. Interrupted placental gas exchange during labour causes hypoxia and acidosis; the baby first gasps, then enters primary apnoea (which responds to drying and stimulation) and then secondary apnoea with falling heart rate, which responds only to ventilation. Effective ventilation of the lungs is therefore the single most important step, and the Navjaat Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (NSSK) teaches the 'golden minute': within the first minute every baby who is not breathing well should either be breathing after initial steps or be receiving bag-and-mask ventilation. Heart rate, counted for 6 seconds and multiplied by 10, guides escalation. Very few babies need chest compressions, intubation or medicines, which require trained help. After resuscitation, babies need warmth, early breastfeeding to prevent hypoglycaemia, monitoring and referral if ventilation exceeded 1 minute.
keyMechanisms: Interrupted placental exchange causes hypoxia, hypercarbia and acidosis.
Primary apnoea responds to stimulation; secondary apnoea needs ventilation.
Lung inflation is the key to raising heart rate.
Hypoxic–ischaemic injury affects brain, kidneys and heart after resuscitation.

symptoms: Not breathing or gasping at birth

redFlags: Heart rate below 60/min after 30 seconds of effective ventilation

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Responds to drying and stimulation within seconds.

clinicalManagement.title: Prepare
actions: Warm room (26–28 °C), radiant warmer on 20 minutes before birth, bag-and-mask and suction checked.

clinicalManagement.title: Initial steps and the golden minute
actions: Dry on the mother's abdomen, position with slight neck extension, clear airway if needed, stimulate and reposition.
Delay cord clamping at least 60 seconds if no resuscitation is needed.
Skin-to-skin, warmth and early breastfeeding.
Start bag-and-mask ventilation within 1 minute.

clinicalManagement.title: Bag-and-mask ventilation
actions: Ventilate at about 40–60 breaths/min (AHA 30–60) with air for term babies; check chest rise and use corrective steps if none after 5 breaths.
Check heart rate after 30 seconds of effective ventilation.

clinicalManagement.title: Escalate
actions: Trained help: chest compressions at 3:1 with 100% oxygen, intubation and medicines per facility NRP chart.

clinicalManagement.title: Stopping and post-resuscitation care
actions: Stop if no signs of life after 10 minutes (NSSK); continue to 30 minutes if signs of life are present.
Refer all babies who needed ventilation for more than 1 minute; keep mother and baby together, warm, and breastfeeding; give vitamin K.

pathophysiology.summary: Low birth weight (under 2,500 g) and preterm birth (under 37 weeks) are the largest contributors to newborn deaths in India. Small babies have little brown fat and a large surface area, so they lose heat quickly; immature suck and swallow coordination, small glycogen stores and immature immunity lead to feeding difficulty, hypoglycaemia and infection; immature lungs and respiratory control cause apnoea and respiratory distress; and immature liver function increases jaundice. Care therefore centres on the warm chain and continuous skin-to-skin Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC) for all stable LBW babies, early and frequent breast milk (by cup, spoon or tube if the baby cannot suck), vitamin K, hygiene, and recognition of danger signs. Babies under 1,800 g, sick babies, those needing tube feeds and those who needed ventilation for over a minute are transferred to a sick newborn care unit.
keyMechanisms: Large surface area and little fat cause rapid heat loss.
Immature suck–swallow and low glycogen cause feeding problems and hypoglycaemia.
Immature immunity increases sepsis risk.
Immature lungs and respiratory control cause distress and apnoea.
